primary_cause: Macro and bank-specific credit-loss fear driven by the biggest payroll drop since 2009. No single fresh JPM headline but investors were repricing banks on recession severity and expected reserve builds
secondary_factors: Payroll collapse and deepening recession forecasts and broad risk-off pressure on financials ahead of earnings season
store_description: JPM's April 3 drop looks mainly tied to the shock labor data with Reuters reporting March payrolls suffered the biggest fall since March 2009. Morgan Stanley was already forecasting a 5.5% full-year U.S. GDP decline and a 38% Q2 contraction.

primary_cause: Rotation out of defensives after the huge April 6 relief rally. No fresh Walmart-specific negative headline in the April 4-6 window
secondary_factors: Concerns that wage bonus and staffing costs would pressure margins and some profit-taking after Walmart had outperformed during the early-pandemic panic
store_description: No fresh Walmart-specific negative headline was found. The stronger explanation is sector rotation after the market jumped over 5% on April 6 with investors shifting toward beaten-down cyclicals while consumer staples lagged the broader rebound.

primary_cause: No clear negative company-specific news. Likely profit-taking/rotation after merger-approval optimism. DOJ approved Schwab's $26 billion TD Ameritrade acquisition on April 2 which was positive
secondary_factors: Concerns about brokerage earnings sensitivity to zero rates and general financial-sector skepticism heading into earnings
store_description: The best stock-specific news in the window was actually positive with Schwab winning DOJ approval for its TD Ameritrade deal on April 2. The April 7 drop most likely reflects profit-taking after approval-related strength plus investor worries that near-zero rates would offset trading-volume benefits.

primary_cause: Rotation out of staples/defensives not negative PG-specific news. No material negative P&G announcement in the April 4-6 window
secondary_factors: Profit-taking after strong defensive outperformance and concern that stockpiling demand might normalize after the initial surge
store_description: Later April results showed P&G's business was actually strong with its best U.S. sales in decades supporting the idea that the April 7 drop was not driven by bad fundamentals. The cleaner explanation is style rotation after stocks surged on April 6.

primary_cause: Lack of a clear stock-specific catalyst. Likely rotation away from defensive/quality industrials amid a sharp risk-on move
secondary_factors: Underlying COVID supply-chain risk to defense production and general industrial exposure fears
store_description: Could not verify a distinct Lockheed headline from April 4-6 that cleanly explains a 3.4% decline. The most likely read is that LMT was caught in a broad risk-on rotation after the April 6 rally.

primary_cause: Likely technical/profit-taking move in a volatile tape rather than stock-specific bad news. No fresh Nvidia-specific negative Reuters item in April 4-6
secondary_factors: Rotation toward more beaten-down cyclicals and ongoing uncertainty around gaming enterprise IT and supply chains under COVID
store_description: No meaningful Nvidia-specific negative headline in the prior three days. Given that the company later guided well above consensus in May the 3.5% decline most likely reflected profit-taking and style rotation rather than a new fundamental shock.

primary_cause: The April 6 737 MAX production cut. Reuters Boeing MAX timeline notes that on April 6 Boeing said it would cut monthly 737 MAX production by nearly 20%
secondary_factors: Air travel collapse from the pandemic and ongoing liquidity and bailout concerns and persistent uncertainty on MAX recertification timing
store_description: BA's April 7 drop has a strong stock-specific explanation with Reuters saying Boeing announced on April 6 that it would reduce monthly 737 MAX production by nearly 20%. That landed on top of air travel demand collapsing under COVID and investors focused on Boeing's cash burn and leverage.

primary_cause: Rotation out of defensive bond-like real estate names. No fresh American Tower-specific negative headline in April 4-6
secondary_factors: Profit-taking after relative outperformance and higher-beta cyclicals attracting capital after the April 6 surge
store_description: There does not appear to have been a company-specific AMT blowup in the three days before the decline. The most plausible explanation is factor rotation with American Tower trading like a defensive yield-like REIT and capital moving into rebound candidates.

secondary_factors: Rotation away from relatively resilient software names and concerns about enterprise spending during lockdowns
store_description: Could not find a clean Adobe-specific negative catalyst. Given later reporting that digital advertising was holding up better than feared the decline most likely reflected portfolio rotation and broad uncertainty around discretionary software spending.

store_description: For GILD there is no decisive bad-news item in the April 4-6 window. Because the important remdesivir data headlines arrived later the decline looks more like investors trimming a crowded COVID-therapy trade and resetting expectations.

secondary_factors: Fear that customer fab spending could be delayed and global supply-chain disruptions from lockdowns
store_description: No AMAT-specific negative catalyst in the three prior days. The drop most likely reflects investor concern that the pandemic would disrupt semiconductor equipment demand and factory expansion plans.

secondary_factors: COVID demand uncertainty across PCs enterprise and industrial end markets and supply-chain worries
store_description: Intel's only notable adjacent headline was actually supportive with a $50 million coronavirus relief commitment. With no clear negative company-specific development INTC's decline is best explained by broad semiconductor and cyclical-growth uncertainty.

secondary_factors: Global manufacturing disruptions and pullback in high-beta tech after sharp swings
store_description: Could not verify a Lam-specific news item in the window. The most plausible explanation is group-level selling in chip-equipment stocks as investors priced in the risk that foundries and memory makers would slow spending or defer expansion plans.

primary_cause: Memory-cycle and end-demand fears amplified by the pandemic. No fresh Micron-specific negative Reuters report in April 6-8
secondary_factors: General semiconductor volatility and concern that enterprise strength would not fully offset consumer weakness
store_description: MU's decline appears more sector- and cycle-driven than event-driven. The best explanation is that investors were discounting a hit to DRAM/NAND demand from the sudden collapse in consumer electronics and broader economic activity.

primary_cause: Pre-earnings fear around bank profits and credit provisions. No singular Morgan Stanley-specific bad headline from April 10-13
secondary_factors: Recession fears from the COVID shutdown and skepticism about investment banking and wealth-management activity and ongoing E*Trade integration risk
store_description: The timing strongly suggests investors were selling large banks ahead of earnings on concern that COVID would trigger heavy reserve builds and a sharp drop in profitability while Morgan Stanley also had overhang from the roughly $13 billion E*Trade acquisition.

primary_cause: Rotation out of defensive utilities. No major NextEra-specific negative news in April 10-13
secondary_factors: Profit-taking after strong relative performance and broader equity-market repositioning as policy and reopening hopes rose
store_description: There does not appear to have been a meaningful NEE-specific negative catalyst. The more convincing explanation is style rotation with utilities giving back some ground as investors tentatively moved back toward cyclicals and growth.

secondary_factors: Merger-integration uncertainty and broad industrial/aerospace weakness tied to airline distress and production cuts
store_description: Even without a single discrete April 10-13 headline RTX's 4.5% decline fits its business mix with the new Raytheon Technologies combining resilient defense operations with heavily pressured commercial-aerospace exposure at exactly the moment air travel had collapsed.

store_description: Unlike the April 7 move the April 13 SCHW drop lines up more clearly with broad financial-sector nerves going into earnings season. Investors were focusing less on the positive DOJ approval and more on how lower net interest margins and integration risk could weigh on results.

primary_cause: Bank earnings/provision fears. No USB-only negative headline in April 10-13
secondary_factors: Regional-bank sensitivity to consumer and commercial credit deterioration and near-zero rates compressing lending margins
store_description: USB's April 13 decline looks mostly like a sector move rather than a company-specific event. Investors were bracing for sizable loan-loss reserves weaker credit quality and margin pressure across the banking sector as the COVID recession deepened.

secondary_factors: Profit-taking after prior outperformance and concern that lower power demand from the economic shutdown could weigh on volumes
